# How often should a decoder-health monitor decide?

**Generated by `scripts/76_decision_rate_curve.py` — do not edit by hand.**

Deciding less often should make monitoring easier for two compounding reasons: a looser per-decision false-positive budget, and more evidence behind each decision. If that holds there is a **decision-rate law** for health monitoring of drifting sensor arrays — detection achievable at a fixed false-flag rate, as a function of how often you decide. **No such curve exists for any system.**

## The curve on the archived data, at a 10% false-flag rate

### T11

| Decisions per hour | Decisions per session | Windows per decision | Detection | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 720 | 55 | 1 | **85.1%** | 62.6% to 98.7% |
| 360 | 27 | 2 | **85.1%** | 62.2% to 98.7% |
| 240 | 18 | 3 | **85.1%** | 62.8% to 98.7% |
| 120 | 9 | 6 | **86.4%** | 65.8% to 98.8% |
| 65 | 5 | 11 | **91.6%** | 74.6% to 99.1% |
| 27 | 2 | 27 | **96.3%** | 79.1% to 99.1% |
| 13 | 1 | 55 | **96.6%** | 80.0% to 98.8% |

Direction: **rises** (+11.5% from the fastest rate to the slowest), on **29 fault-free episodes**.

### T5

| Decisions per hour | Decisions per session | Windows per decision | Detection | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 720 | 42 | 1 | **86.4%** | 66.9% to 93.8% |
| 360 | 21 | 2 | **86.2%** | 69.1% to 94.3% |
| 240 | 14 | 3 | **85.4%** | 70.7% to 95.1% |
| 120 | 7 | 6 | **86.2%** | 67.5% to 95.9% |
| 65 | 3 | 11 | **78.3%** | 71.5% to 91.1% |
| 27 | 1 | 27 | **68.3%** | 42.3% to 75.6% |

Direction: **falls** (-18.2% from the fastest rate to the slowest), on **21 fault-free episodes**.

## Why this cannot be settled here

**The two participants disagree about the direction of the curve.** On T11 it rises; on T5 it falls. A law that points one way in one array and the other way in the next is not a law, it is two noisy measurements.

**And the threshold rests on almost nothing.** The false-flag rate is set from genuinely fault-free episodes, and there are 29 (T11) and 21 (T5). At a 10% rate the threshold is the 90% quantile of that — two or three episodes in the tail. The confidence intervals above show what that costs.

Those are not reasons to drop the question. **They are a specification for the measurement that would answer it**, and it is a measurement no existing dataset can provide, because it needs hundreds of fault-free sessions with constructed onsets.

## What the rig measures, and why one campaign is enough

**The decision rate is an analysis choice, not a recording choice.** A session recorded once can be scored at every decision rate afterwards. So the rig campaign does not need an arm per rate — it needs enough fault-free sessions to put a trustworthy threshold on the tail, and the whole curve falls out of the same recordings.

| | Archived data | Rig campaign (B-14) |
|---|---|---|
| Fault-free sessions | 29 / 21 | **101** |
| Onsets | not recorded; chosen by the analyst afterwards | **drawn and written down before each session** |
| Arrays | 2, from one deposit | as many as are built |
| Who collected it | Pun et al., 2024 | **this project** |
| Can it settle the direction of the curve? | **no** | yes |

That last row is the point. The archived data raised this question and cannot answer it. **The rig answers it with data this project collects itself**, and the answer is a design curve that applies to any many-channel sensor that drifts, not only to brain implants.

## What would falsify the law

If the rig's curve is **flat**, deciding less often does not help and the failure is in the detector rather than the sampling — which sends the next attempt somewhere completely different from where this project would have sent it.

If the curve **falls**, as T5's does, pooling windows destroys more information than it buys, and the right move is the opposite of the one this analysis suggests. **That outcome is why the curve has to be measured rather than argued for.**
